subject: biology
prompt: A cell is about to divide into two. Why must it first make a copy of its DNA?

image.alt: Animation of a cell copying its DNA before dividing into two cells

options.text: So that the cell can stop doing respiration while it divides
So that each daughter cell gets the information (blueprint) for the body design
So that only one daughter cell gets DNA and the other keeps the cell machinery
So that the cell becomes larger without dividing

hint: Chromosomes in the nucleus carry the information that is inherited by the next generation.
explanation: DNA in the nucleus is the information source for making proteins, so it is the **blueprint of the body design**. Reproduction therefore starts with a DNA copy, and DNA copying is accompanied by making extra cellular apparatus so that each copy ends up in a cell that can run life processes. Keeping one copy and pushing the other out would not work, because the pushed-out copy would have no organised cell structure.

subject: biology
prompt: In **budding**, a small outgrowth develops. Later it separates and becomes a new individual. Which picture shows budding?

options.text: Picture A

image.alt: A cell splitting into two equal halves

options.text: Picture B

image.alt: A sac on a stalk releasing spores

options.text: Picture C

image.alt: A cell with a small bud growing from its side

options.text: Picture D

image.alt: A green filament breaking into pieces

hint: Look for an unequal outgrowth on the side of the parent.
explanation: In **budding** (yeast, Hydra) a small bud grows from the parent at one site, grows further and then detaches as a new individual. Picture A is **binary fission**, where the parent splits into two equal halves. Picture B is **spore formation** (as in *Rhizopus*) and picture D is **fragmentation** (as in *Spirogyra*).

subject: biology
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Heat-resistant bacteria survive when water warms while other bacteria die

assertion: Variation is useful for the survival of a species over time.
reason: If the environment changes a lot, a few variants (slightly different individuals) in the population may be able to survive and grow further.
hint: Think about what happens to bacteria when water warms because of global warming.
explanation: Both statements are true and R is the reason for A. Copying of DNA is never perfectly accurate, so a population contains variants. If a niche changes (for example the water warms up), most bacteria may die but the few **heat-resistant variants** survive and multiply. Variation need not help every individual, but it helps the **species** to survive.

subject: biology
prompt: The picture shows a Plasmodium cell dividing. How is this different from binary fission in Amoeba?

image.alt: Plasmodium cell dividing into many daughter cells at once

options.text: One parent cell divides into many daughter cells at the same time
Only two daughter cells are formed, but they are of unequal size
Two parent cells join together before dividing
The DNA of the parent is not copied before the division

hint: Count the daughter cells in the picture.
explanation: In **binary fission** one cell splits into two. In **multiple fission**, as in the malarial parasite *Plasmodium*, the nucleus divides many times and the cell splits into **many daughter cells simultaneously**. Both are asexual (one parent) and both need DNA copying first, so the last two options are wrong.

subject: biology
prompt: In Amoeba, the cell can split in any plane (direction). But in Leishmania (which causes kala-azar), binary fission happens in a fixed direction. Why?

image.alt: Leishmania cell with a whip-like tail dividing along its length

options.text: Leishmania is a multicellular organism with tissues
Leishmania reproduces by forming spores instead
Amoeba has no nucleus, so it splits anywhere
Leishmania has a whip-like structure at one end, so its body is more organised

hint: Look at the structure at the top of each Leishmania cell.
explanation: Some unicellular organisms show more body organisation. Leishmania has a **whip-like structure at one end**, and binary fission happens in a fixed direction in relation to it. Amoeba has an irregular shape without such a structure, so it can divide in any plane. Both are single-celled, have a nucleus and divide by fission, not by spores.

subject: biology
prompt: When *Spirogyra* becomes mature, it breaks up into smaller pieces. Each piece grows into a new filament. Why can this simple organism do this?

image.alt: Spirogyra filament breaking into pieces that grow into new filaments

options.text: It has specialised organs that are placed at fixed positions
Its body organisation is relatively simple, so each fragment can grow into a new individual
It is a single cell, so it divides by multiple fission
The pieces first need to fuse with pieces of another filament

hint: Think about what stops complex organisms from simply breaking up.
explanation: **Fragmentation** works in multicellular organisms with a simple body design such as *Spirogyra*. Complex organisms have cells organised into tissues and organs at definite positions, so cell-by-cell division or breaking up would be impractical. Fragmentation involves one parent only, so no fusion is needed.

subject: biology
prompt: In Hydra, a bud develops on the body. It grows into a tiny individual and later detaches (separates). How does the bud form?

image.alt: Hydra with a bud growing from its side

options.text: As an outgrowth due to repeated cell division at one specific site, using regenerative cells
By two Hydra joining their bodies and exchanging cells
By the whole body breaking into many pieces
By a spore case bursting and releasing spores

hint: A bud is a localised outgrowth of the parent body.
explanation: Hydra uses its **regenerative cells** for **budding**. Repeated cell division at one site makes an outgrowth (the bud), which becomes a small individual and detaches when mature. Breaking into pieces is regeneration/fragmentation, and spore formation uses spore cases as in *Rhizopus*.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the **bud**. It will mature and detach (separate) to become a new independent Hydra.

image.alt: Hydra with tentacles, a bud on its side and a foot attached to a stone

hint: It is the small outgrowth on the side of the body.
explanation: The **bud** is an outgrowth formed by repeated cell division at one site on the parent. When fully grown it detaches and lives independently. The tentacles catch food, the body column is the parent, and the foot holds the animal in place.

subject: biology
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A Planaria cut into pieces with each piece regrowing into a whole worm

assertion: Regeneration is the same as reproduction.
reason: If a Planaria is cut into pieces, each piece can grow into a complete organism.
hint: Ask whether Planaria normally depend on being cut up to reproduce.
explanation: A is **false**: regeneration is not the same as reproduction because most organisms would not normally depend on being cut up in order to reproduce. R is **true**: Planaria and Hydra can be cut into pieces and each piece grows into a complete organism. Regeneration is carried out by specialised cells that proliferate and then change into various cell types in an organised sequence called development.

subject: biology
prompt: Arrange the steps by which a cut piece of Planaria becomes a whole worm.

image.alt: A Planaria cut into three pieces regrowing into complete worms

items.text: The cells change into various cell types and tissues in an organised sequence
A Planaria is cut into several pieces
Each piece has become a complete new worm
Specialised cells in each piece divide to make a large number of cells

hint: Cells must multiply before they can specialise.
explanation: After cutting, **specialised cells proliferate** and make a mass of cells. Different cells in this mass then **change into various cell types and tissues** in an organised sequence called development. Finally each piece is a complete organism.

subject: biology
prompt: Anita cuts a potato into pieces. Some pieces have a notch (eye) and some do not. She keeps them on wet cotton. As the picture shows, only the pieces with a notch give fresh green shoots and roots. Why?

image.alt: Potato pieces on wet cotton, only the piece with an eye sprouting

options.text: The pieces with a notch contain more stored food
Water enters a piece faster through the notch
The notch contains tiny seeds of the potato
The notch is a bud, and a new shoot and roots can develop only from a bud

hint: What does a plant part need in order to develop a new shoot?
explanation: In **vegetative propagation**, a plant part grows into a new plant only if it carries a **bud**. The notches (eyes) of a potato are buds, so only pieces with an eye sprout. All pieces have stored food and take up water, and a potato tuber contains no seeds, so these cannot explain the difference.

subject: biology
prompt: Two pieces are cut from a money plant. Piece A has a node with a leaf. Piece B is cut from between two nodes. Both are kept with one end in water. As the picture shows, only piece A grows roots and fresh leaves. Why?

image.alt: Two money plant cuttings in water, A with a node and leaf and B cut between nodes

options.text: Piece B has more stem, so it rots in the water
Piece A carries a node, where a bud is present from which new growth starts
Piece A is longer and stores more water
Piece A contains a seed inside its leaf

hint: Think about where buds are found on a stem.
explanation: New roots and shoots arise from a **node**, where a bud is present. Piece B, cut between two nodes, has no bud and does not grow. This is why cuttings of money plant, rose or sugarcane are cut so that they carry nodes. Length, water storage and seeds have nothing to do with it; a leaf does not contain seeds.

subject: biology
prompt: Which of these are advantages of vegetative propagation? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Bryophyllum leaf with plantlets growing at its notches

options.text: Plants can bear flowers and fruits earlier than plants raised from seeds
It creates a lot of new variation by combining two parents
All the plants produced are genetically similar to the parent and have all its characteristics
It needs pollination and fertilisation before new plants can grow
Plants like banana, orange, rose and jasmine that have lost the capacity to produce seeds can still be grown

hint: Only one parent is involved, and no seeds are needed.
explanation: Vegetative propagation (layering, grafting, cuttings) lets plants like sugarcane, roses and grapes be grown with **earlier flowering**, **genetic similarity** to the parent, and even for plants such as banana, orange, rose and jasmine that **cannot make seeds**. It involves one parent, so it does not combine variations, and it needs no pollination or fertilisation.

subject: biology
prompt: Mould grows on a moist slice of bread. Which structures are involved in its reproduction?

image.alt: Bread mould with thread-like hyphae and blob-on-a-stick structures releasing spores

options.text: The thread-like hyphae spreading on the bread
The slice of bread itself
The tiny blob-on-a-stick sporangia that contain spores
The hyphae and sporangia are both only for absorbing food

hint: The reproductive parts are the blobs held up on stalks.
explanation: In *Rhizopus* the thread-like **hyphae** are not reproductive parts. The blobs are **sporangia** that contain **spores**. Spores have thick walls that protect them until they land on another moist surface, where they grow into new mould individuals.

subject: biology
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Spores rising from sporangia of bread mould

assertion: The spores of Rhizopus can survive in unfavourable (bad) conditions until they reach a moist surface.
reason: Spores are covered by thick walls that protect them.
hint: What does a thick wall do for a tiny cell?
explanation: Both statements are true and R explains A. The **thick wall** protects the spore, so it can wait until it contacts a moist surface, where it can germinate and grow into a new *Rhizopus*. This is an advantage of reproducing by spores.

subject: biology
prompt: In tissue culture, cells from the growing tip of a plant are placed in an artificial medium (a food mixture made in the lab). What is a **callus**?

image.alt: Tissue culture: shoot tip cells, callus, plantlets and plants in soil

options.text: A small group of rapidly dividing cells formed on the artificial medium
A seed formed in the culture jar
A tiny plantlet already ready to be planted in soil
The hormone that makes plantlets grow

hint: It forms before the plantlets do.
explanation: The cells divide rapidly to form a small group of cells called a **callus**. The callus is then moved to a medium containing **hormones** for growth and differentiation, and the plantlets are planted in soil. Many disease-free plants can be grown from one parent, commonly ornamental plants.

subject: biology
prompt: Arrange the steps of tissue culture in the correct order.

image.alt: A laboratory jar with plant tissue growing on an artificial medium

items.text: The cells divide rapidly on an artificial medium to form a callus
Tissue or cells are taken from the growing tip of a plant
The plantlets are placed in soil and grow into mature plants
The callus is moved to a medium containing hormones for growth and differentiation

hint: Soil is the last stage.
explanation: Cells are separated from the **growing tip**, they divide to form a **callus** on a nutrient medium, the callus is transferred to a **hormone medium** for growth and differentiation into plantlets, and finally the plantlets go into **soil**.

subject: biology
prompt: Match each organism with its mode of asexual reproduction.

image.alt: A cell splitting into two equal halves
One cell dividing into many small cells at once
A cell with a small bud growing from its side
A green filament breaking into pieces
A sac on a stalk releasing spores

right.text: Binary fission
Multiple fission
Budding
Fragmentation
Spore formation

hint: Plasmodium divides into many cells at once.
explanation: *Amoeba* splits into two (**binary fission**), *Plasmodium* into many cells together (**multiple fission**), yeast puts out small **buds**, *Spirogyra* breaks into **fragments**, and *Rhizopus* forms **spores** in sporangia. All are asexual because only one individual is needed.

subject: biology
prompt: Which of these are examples of **asexual** reproduction? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Asexual reproduction from one parent versus sexual reproduction from two parents

options.text: Hydra forming a bud
Spirogyra breaking into fragments
A sperm fusing with an egg
Rhizopus releasing spores
A bull and a cow producing a calf

hint: Asexual reproduction needs only one individual.
explanation: Budding in Hydra, fragmentation in *Spirogyra* and spore formation in *Rhizopus* all create new generations from a **single individual**. Fusion of a sperm and an egg, and a bull and a cow producing a calf, need **two individuals (male and female)**, so they are sexual.

subject: biology
prompt: The picture shows that gametes have half the chromosomes of body cells. Suppose gametes had the same number of chromosomes as body cells. What would happen in each new generation?

image.alt: Gametes with half the chromosomes fuse to form a zygote with the full number

options.text: Nothing would change, as the extra DNA would be thrown away
The zygote would have double the chromosomes and DNA, and this would keep doubling
The number of chromosomes would keep decreasing
Gametes would not be formed at all

hint: A zygote gets DNA from both parents.
explanation: If each new generation is a combination of DNA from two individuals, it would have **twice the DNA** of the previous one, which would upset the control of the cell by its DNA. This is solved by a special cell division, **meiosis**, in germ-cell lineages, which gives gametes half the number of chromosomes and half the DNA. Fusion of two gametes then restores the original number.

subject: biology
prompt: Look at the two germ-cells X and Y. Which statement is correct?

image.alt: A large round cell X with food granules and a small tailed cell Y

options.text: X is the male gamete because it is larger
Y is the female gamete because it can move
X is the female gamete containing stored food; Y is the smaller, motile male gamete
X and Y are both female gametes

hint: Which germ-cell stores food and which one moves?
explanation: As body designs become more complex, germ-cells specialise: one is **large and contains food stores** (the female gamete) and the other is **smaller and motile** (the male gamete). The food store helps the zygote to grow into an organism with specialised tissues and organs.

subject: biology
prompt: Flower A has only stamens. Flower B has only a pistil. Flower C has both. Which flowers are **unisexual**?

image.alt: Three flowers: A with stamens only, B with pistil only, C with both

options.text: A and B
A and C
B and C
C only

hint: A unisexual flower has either stamens or pistil, not both.
explanation: A flower is **unisexual** (papaya, watermelon) when it has either stamens or pistil, and **bisexual** (hibiscus, mustard) when it has both. A and B are unisexual; C is bisexual.

subject: biology
prompt: The pollen grains must land on a suitable stigma. Tap the **stigma**.

image.alt: Longitudinal section of a flower with pollen drifting to the stigma

hint: It is the terminal part of the pistil and may be sticky.
explanation: The pistil is made of the **ovary** (swollen bottom), the **style** (middle elongated part) and the **stigma** (terminal part, which may be sticky). Pollen has to be transferred to the stigma.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the part that produces the yellowish **pollen grains**.

image.alt: Longitudinal section of a flower showing its parts

hint: The stamen is the male reproductive part.
explanation: The **stamen** is the male reproductive part and its **anther** produces the yellowish pollen grains that stick to our hands if we touch it. Pollen carries the male germ-cell; the ovary holds the ovules with the egg cells.

subject: biology
prompt: Match each part of a flower with its role.

image.alt: Longitudinal section of a flower

right.text: Produces pollen grains
Terminal part of the pistil that receives pollen
Elongated middle part through which the pollen tube grows
Swollen bottom part that contains ovules

hint: The pollen tube travels down the middle of the pistil.
explanation: The **anther** makes pollen, the **stigma** receives it, the **style** is the passage for the pollen tube, and the **ovary** contains the **ovules**, each with an egg cell. Fertilisation happens in the ovule.

subject: biology
prompt: Which picture shows **cross-pollination**?

options.text: Picture A

image.alt: Pollen moving to the stigma of the same flower

options.text: Picture B

image.alt: A pollen grain growing a tube inside the style

options.text: Picture C

image.alt: A seed sprouting in soil

options.text: Picture D

image.alt: Pollen carried from one flower to a different flower

hint: Cross means from one flower to a different flower.
explanation: In **cross-pollination** pollen is transferred from one flower to another by agents such as wind, water or animals. Picture A shows **self-pollination** (same flower). Picture B shows a pollen tube growing after pollination, and picture C shows germination of a seed.

subject: biology
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Longitudinal section of a flower with pollen reaching the stigma

assertion: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma.
reason: Pollination is the fusion of the male gamete with the female gamete to form a zygote.
hint: Fusion of germ-cells has a different name.
explanation: A is **true** and R is **false**. Pollination is only the **transfer of pollen** to the stigma. The fusion of germ-cells to form the zygote is **fertilisation**, which happens later in the ovule after the pollen tube reaches it.

subject: biology
prompt: After pollen lands on the stigma, a tube grows out of the pollen grain. Through which part does it travel to reach the ovary?

image.alt: A pollen grain growing a tube down the style to the ovule

options.text: Filament
Style
Sepal
Petal

hint: It is the elongated middle part of the pistil.
explanation: The **pollen tube** grows from the pollen grain through the **style** to reach the ovary, where the male germ-cell fuses with the female gamete in the ovule. The filament holds the anther, while sepals and petals are not part of the pistil.

subject: biology
prompt: Arrange the events from pollination to seed formation.

image.alt: A pollen tube growing toward an ovule

items.text: The zygote divides several times to form an embryo in the ovule
A pollen grain lands on the stigma
The ovule develops a tough coat and becomes a seed
A pollen tube grows through the style to the ovary
The male germ-cell fuses with the female gamete in the ovule

hint: Fertilisation gives the zygote.
explanation: Pollen lands on the stigma (**pollination**), grows a tube through the style, and the male germ-cell fuses with the egg in the ovule (**fertilisation**) to form the **zygote**. The zygote divides to form an **embryo**, and the ovule develops a tough coat to become a **seed**.

subject: biology
prompt: After fertilisation in a flowering plant, which parts of the flower become the seed and the fruit?

image.alt: Ovule becomes the seed and ovary becomes the fruit after fertilisation

options.text: The ovary becomes the seed and the ovule becomes the fruit
The stigma becomes the seed and the style becomes the fruit
The ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit
The petals become the fruit and the sepals become the seed

hint: The ovary ripens, while the ovule develops a tough coat.
explanation: The **ovule** (with the embryo) develops a tough coat and becomes the **seed**. The **ovary** grows rapidly and ripens to form the **fruit**. Petals, sepals, stamens, style and stigma may shrivel and fall off.

subject: biology
prompt: A soaked Bengal gram (chana) seed is opened. Tap the part that will grow into the **root** of the seedling.

image.alt: An opened gram seed showing seed coat, cotyledons, plumule and radicle

hint: It points downwards, away from the shoot.
explanation: The seed contains the future plant, the **embryo**, which grows into a seedling under suitable conditions (**germination**). The **radicle** becomes the root, the **plumule** becomes the shoot, and the **cotyledons** store food. The seed coat protects the seed.

subject: biology
prompt: Which changes appear at puberty in **both** boys and girls? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Graph showing body growth slowing as reproductive tissues mature

options.text: The voice begins to crack
Thick hair grows in the armpits and genital area
The skin becomes oily and pimples may appear
Menstruation begins
Thinner hair appears on legs and arms

hint: Two options are specific to one sex only.
explanation: Changes common to both: thick hair in armpits and the genital area, oily skin and pimples, and thinner hair on legs and arms. **Voice cracking** (and thick facial hair) are seen in boys, while **menstruation** starts in girls. Puberty is when reproductive tissue matures as the rate of general body growth slows.

subject: biology
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Human male reproductive system

assertion: The testes are located outside the abdominal cavity, in the scrotum.
reason: The testes secrete the hormone testosterone.
hint: Is testosterone the reason the testes hang outside?
explanation: Both statements are true but R does **not** explain A. The testes lie in the scrotum because **sperm formation needs a temperature lower than the normal body temperature**. Testosterone regulates sperm formation and brings about the changes seen in boys at puberty, but it has nothing to do with the position of the testes.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the organ in which **sperms are formed**.

image.alt: Human male reproductive system seen from the front

hint: These organs lie in the scrotum.
explanation: Sperms are formed in the **testes**, which are in the scrotum outside the abdominal cavity. The vas deferens carries sperms, while the seminal vesicles and prostate add fluid secretions.

subject: biology
prompt: Sperms and urine both pass through one **common passage**. Tap this passage.

image.alt: Human male reproductive system seen from the front

hint: The vas deferens unites with a tube coming from the urinary bladder.
explanation: The vas deferens joins a tube from the urinary bladder, so the **urethra** forms a common passage for both **sperms and urine**. The bladder only stores urine, and the vas deferens carries only sperms.

subject: biology
prompt: Match each part of the male reproductive system with its function.

image.alt: Human male reproductive system

right.text: Forms sperms and secretes testosterone
Delivers sperms from the testis
Add secretions so sperms are in a fluid that eases transport and gives nutrition
Common passage for sperms and urine
Holds the testes outside the body at a lower temperature

hint: Two of the functions are about carrying, but in different tubes.
explanation: The **testes** form sperms and secrete **testosterone**; the **vas deferens** delivers sperms; the **prostate and seminal vesicles** add fluid that eases transport and provides nutrition; the **urethra** is common to sperms and urine; the **scrotum** keeps the testes at the lower temperature that sperm formation needs.

subject: biology
prompt: Arrange the path taken by sperms in the male body.

image.alt: Human male reproductive system

items.text: The sperms pass through the urethra
Sperms are formed in the testes
The sperms leave through the penis
The prostate gland and seminal vesicles add their secretions, forming a fluid
The sperms travel through the vas deferens

hint: Secretions are added along the path of the vas deferens.
explanation: Sperms form in the **testes**, move through the **vas deferens**, and on the way glands such as the **prostate** and **seminal vesicles** add fluid. They then travel through the **urethra** and leave through the penis.

subject: biology
prompt: The sperms travel upwards and may meet the egg in a thin tube. Tap the part where **fertilisation** takes place.

image.alt: Human female reproductive system seen from the front

hint: The egg is carried from the ovary to the womb through this thin tube.
explanation: Fertilisation occurs in the **fallopian tube (oviduct)**. The egg released by an ovary travels along it, and the sperms reach it from the vagina through the uterus. The fertilised egg (zygote) then begins to divide.

subject: biology
prompt: The fertilised egg divides into a ball of cells. This **embryo is implanted** (gets attached) in the lining of an organ and grows there. Tap that organ.

image.alt: Human female reproductive system seen from the front

hint: It is an elastic bag-like structure formed by the union of the two oviducts.
explanation: The embryo is implanted in the lining of the **uterus**, where it grows and develops organs to become a foetus. The uterus prepares itself every month, with a thick lining supplied richly with blood, to nourish the growing embryo. The cervix is the opening of the uterus into the vagina.

subject: biology
prompt: Match each part of the female reproductive system with what it does.

image.alt: Human female reproductive system

right.text: Makes eggs and some hormones
Carries the egg from the ovary and is where it may meet sperms
Bag-like organ where the embryo is implanted and grows
Narrow opening through which the uterus opens into the vagina
Passage through which sperms enter the female body

hint: The uterus opens into the vagina through the cervix.
explanation: The **ovaries** make eggs (one a month) and some hormones. The egg travels through the **fallopian tube**. The **uterus** nurtures the embryo and opens into the **vagina** through the **cervix**; sperms enter through the vaginal passage.

subject: biology
prompt: Which picture shows the **motile male germ-cell** (sperm) of human beings?

options.text: Picture A

image.alt: A large round cell with food granules

options.text: Picture B

image.alt: A tiny cell with a head and a long tail

options.text: Picture C

image.alt: A yellow bumpy round grain

options.text: Picture D

image.alt: A sac on a stalk releasing spores

hint: Sperms are tiny and consist mainly of genetic material and a long tail.
explanation: A sperm has mainly **genetic material** and a long **tail** that helps it swim to the female germ-cell. Picture A is the large egg with food stores, picture C is a pollen grain (the male germ-cell of a plant is produced by pollen grains), and picture D shows spores of a fungus.

subject: biology
prompt: Why does menstruation occur in a woman who is not pregnant?

image.alt: Menstrual cycle in which the uterine lining thickens and breaks down if the egg is not fertilised

options.text: The ovary stops making eggs for a month
The fertilised egg is pushed out of the uterus
Sperms die in the uterus and are removed with blood
The thick, spongy uterine lining, prepared for an embryo, is not needed if the egg is not fertilised, so it breaks and leaves as blood and mucus

hint: The uterus prepares itself every month for an embryo.
explanation: The ovary releases an egg every month and the uterus prepares for it by thickening its lining, which becomes spongy and rich in blood. If the egg (which lives for about a day) is **not fertilised**, this lining is not needed, so it slowly breaks and comes out through the vagina as blood and mucus. This cycle, **menstruation**, lasts about two to eight days.

subject: biology
prompt: Tap the **placenta**. It is a special disc embedded in the uterine wall. It nourishes (feeds) the embryo.

image.alt: Uterus cross-section with a foetus, umbilical cord and placenta

hint: It is the dark red disc fixed to the wall of the uterus.
explanation: The **placenta** is a disc embedded in the uterine wall. It has **villi** on the embryo's side and blood spaces on the mother's side, giving a large surface area for exchange of glucose, oxygen and wastes between the mother's blood and the embryo.

subject: biology
prompt: Which statements about the placenta are correct? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Placenta joining the foetus and the mother

options.text: Glucose and oxygen pass from the mother's blood to the embryo through it
It makes a new egg every month
Waste substances made by the embryo are passed into the mother's blood through it
It has villi on the embryo's side that give a large surface area
It is a tube that carries the egg from the ovary to the uterus

hint: It is the link between the embryo and the mother's blood.
explanation: The placenta has **villi** on the embryo's side and **blood spaces** on the mother's side. This provides a large surface area for **glucose and oxygen** to pass to the embryo and for **wastes** to be removed into the mother's blood. Eggs are made in the ovary, and the fallopian tube carries the egg.

subject: biology
prompt: Arrange the stages from fertilisation to the birth of a child.

image.alt: A foetus inside the uterus joined to the placenta

items.text: The embryo develops organs and becomes a foetus, nourished through the placenta
The zygote divides to form a ball of cells, the embryo
The child is born by rhythmic contractions of the uterine muscles
A sperm fertilises the egg in the oviduct, forming a zygote
The embryo is implanted in the lining of the uterus

hint: A zygote exists only after fertilisation.
explanation: Fertilisation forms the **zygote**, which divides into a ball of cells (**embryo**). The embryo is **implanted** in the thick uterine lining, grows into a **foetus** nourished through the placenta over about nine months, and the child is born by **rhythmic contractions** of uterine muscles.

subject: biology
prompt: Some contraceptive devices are **placed in the uterus** to prevent pregnancy. Which picture shows such a device?

options.text: Picture A

subject: biology
prompt: Match each contraceptive method with how it prevents pregnancy.

image.alt: A thin sheath worn over the penis
Tablets taken by mouth
A T-shaped device placed in the uterus
A cut and blocked tube

right.text: Mechanical barrier so that sperm cannot reach the egg
Changes hormonal balance so eggs are not released
Placed in the uterus to prevent pregnancy
Blocks the vas deferens or the fallopian tube

hint: Hormones are involved in only one of the four.
explanation: A **condom** is a barrier; **pills** act on hormones so eggs are not released; a **copper-T** sits in the uterus; and **surgery** blocks the vas deferens (male) or the fallopian tube (female) so fertilisation cannot occur.

subject: biology
prompt: Which statements about contraception are **true**? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Four contraceptive methods: condom, pills, copper-T and a surgical block

options.text: A copper-T protects the user from sexually transmitted diseases
Using a condom helps to prevent transmission of many infections to some extent
Oral pills change hormonal balance and can cause side-effects
Blocking the vas deferens stops sperms from being formed in the testes
Surgical methods are safe in the long run but can cause infections if not performed properly

hint: Think about what each method actually does.
explanation: A condom is a barrier that helps to prevent many infections to some extent, **oral pills** change hormonal balance and may have side-effects, and **surgery** is safe in the long run but can cause infection if done improperly. A copper-T does **not** prevent STDs, and blocking the vas deferens only stops sperm transfer; sperms are still made in the testes.

prompt: A woman is using a copper-T. She asks if it will also protect her from sexually transmitted infections such as gonorrhoea, syphilis or HIV-AIDS. What is the correct answer?

image.alt: Condom, pills, copper-T and a surgical block as methods to avoid pregnancy

options.text: Yes, because it is placed in the uterus and kills germs there
Yes, because it changes her hormonal balance
No. It helps to prevent pregnancy but does not protect against such infections; a condom helps to some extent
No, because it blocks the fallopian tube and causes the infection

hint: Which contraceptive is a barrier between two bodies?
explanation: A **copper-T** is placed in the uterus and only prevents pregnancy. Infections such as gonorrhoea and syphilis (bacterial) and warts and HIV-AIDS (viral) spread by sexual contact, and a **condom** (a covering for the penis) can help prevent transmission to some extent. The copper-T does not act on hormones or block tubes.

options.text: The use of condoms and pills
The use of copper-T devices
Menstruation occurring every month
Illegal sex-selective abortion of female foetuses (female foeticide)

hint: Prenatal sex determination is prohibited by law.
explanation: Surgery can be misused to remove unwanted pregnancies, as in illegal **sex-selective abortion of female foetuses**. This is making the child sex ratio decline, even though **prenatal sex determination is prohibited by law**. For a healthy society the female-male sex ratio must be maintained.
